channel.title: Theraglee checklists
channel.description: Free mental health checklists from Theraglee, two new ones a day.

item.title: Planning the Holidays Before They Arrive
item.description: For the weeks before the holidays, when invitations, money and expectations all land at once. It settles what you say yes to, what you spend, how long you stay, and where the ordinary days sit in among the gatherings. Items: Decide now which invitations you will accept · Pick the number you will spend before you shop · Name the one tradition that actually matters to you · Plan for the empty chair if there is one · Agree your leaving time before you arrive · Keep one ordinary day in the middle · Write down the questions you know you will be asked · Ask for one job to do at the gathering · Put the week after it on the calendar now.

item.title: Sleeping Well When You Work Nights
item.description: For anyone working nights or rotating shifts, when sleep has to happen at the wrong time of day. It sets one sleep window, makes the room dark, times the caffeine and the meals, and keeps an hour a week for people. Items: Pick one sleep window and keep it on days off · Make the bedroom fully dark before you lie down · Wear sunglasses on the drive home · Put the phone in another room on silent · Eat your main meal before the shift, not during it · Stop the caffeine six hours before your sleep window · Tell the household your sleep hours in writing · Keep one fixed hour a week with people you like · Write down how many hours you actually got · Ask about the pattern before you agree to swap a shift.

item.title: The First Month After a Separation
item.description: For the first month after a separation, when everything needs deciding at once. It settles who tells whom, puts the money and the paperwork in set hours, keeps the children's version of events the same from both sides, and lets a flat week be flat. Items: Decide who tells which people · Separate the money before the feelings · Write down what the children are told · Pick one friend for the late nights · Keep the house running on a short list · Stop rereading the messages · Put one hour a week on the paperwork · Let a flat week be the week it is · Say nothing you would not want repeated.

item.title: When a Parent Starts Needing Help
item.description: For the point where a parent starts needing help and nobody has said so. It gets what you have noticed written down, asks them what they want first, walks the house for hazards, and divides the jobs with your siblings in writing. Items: Write down what you have actually noticed · Ask them what they want before deciding · Walk the house for the obvious hazards · Get the paperwork named while it is easy · Ask to be at the next appointment · Divide the jobs with your siblings in writing · Find out what the county offers · Keep one visit that is not about care · Say out loud what you cannot do.

item.title: The First Weeks With a Newborn
item.description: For the first weeks with a newborn, when the days have no shape. It gets feeds and diapers on one sheet, puts visitors behind a rule, splits the night into named shifts, and keeps the parent's own checkup on the calendar. Items: Write feeds and diapers on one sheet · Let someone else cook one meal a day · Put visitors behind a clear rule · Split the night into shifts you name · Get outside once, even to the mailbox · Keep your own checkup on the calendar · Expect the evening to be the hard part · Send the small question to the pediatrician · Call 1-833-TLC-MAMA if the dark stays.

item.title: When Your Faith Feels Far Away
item.description: For a stretch when the practice feels empty and you are not sure what is left. It asks for the smallest version rather than the whole thing, the honest words rather than the right ones, and treats dryness as part of a long tradition. Items: Go once without waiting to feel like it · Keep the smallest version of the practice · Say the honest thing rather than the right one · Read something old you used to love · Tell one person in the community · Do one thing for someone quietly · Let the doubt be part of it, not the end · Ask what else is tired.

item.title: Getting Back Into Reading
item.description: For wanting to read again when the phone keeps winning. It puts a book where the phone usually sits, counts five pages as reading, gives you permission to abandon one you are not enjoying, and lets the audiobook count. Items: Keep one book in the bag you always carry · Count five pages as reading · Put the book where the phone usually sits · Abandon the one you are not enjoying · Read the first ten pages in the store · Get a library card and borrow three · Let the audiobook count · Tell one person what you are reading.

item.title: Taking Your Medication Every Day
item.description: For a daily medication you keep forgetting or putting off. It ties the dose to something you already do, puts the refill a week ahead of the gap, keeps the side effects written down, and leaves stopping to a conversation with the prescriber. Items: Tie it to something you already do · Use a box with the days on it · Set the alarm for the same minute daily · Order the refill when a week is left · Keep one dose where you get caught out · Write side effects down with the date · Ask the pharmacist about the awkward part · Never stop because you feel better · Say so if the cost is the problem.

item.title: When Your Teenager Will Not Talk to You
item.description: For a stretch when a teenager has gone quiet and every question makes it worse. It trades the interview for one ordinary comment a day, moves the talking sideways into a car or a walk, and keeps your first reaction off your face. Items: Say one ordinary thing a day with no question in it · Take the conversation sideways · Ask about the thing, not the feeling · Let the silence last longer than is comfortable · Keep the first reaction off your face · Separate the rule from the relationship · Say what you are not going to do about it · Make sure one other adult is around · Say the door is open and then stop saying it.

item.title: Putting Down the Cigarettes
item.description: For the week you decide to stop smoking. It sets a date with witnesses, gets real help from a pharmacist, plans the three hardest cigarettes of the day, clears what is within reach, and treats one lapse as one cigarette rather than a return. Items: Pick the date and tell two people · Ask the pharmacist what to use · Name the three hardest cigarettes of your day · Clear the car, the lighters and the ashtray · Decide what your hands will do instead · Change the route that goes past the store · Put the money somewhere you can see it · Treat one cigarette as one cigarette · Call 1-800-QUIT-NOW when it gets loud.

item.title: The First Week of Looking for Work
item.description: For the first week of looking for work, before the routine exists. It gives the search office hours instead of the whole day, trades thirty applications for three good ones, keeps one sheet of what went where, and expects silence more often than a no. Items: Give it office hours, not all day · Send three good applications, not thirty · Keep one sheet of what you sent and when · Rewrite the top third for each job · Message one person a day you already know · Expect silence more often than a no · Put one thing in the week that is not the search · Say the number you need out loud · Stop at a set time each day.

item.title: Pacing a Week With a Long-Term Condition
item.description: For living with a condition whose cost varies, where a good day borrows from tomorrow. It treats energy as a budget, puts the rest in the calendar before the plans, splits the big job across three days, and keeps a short note of what cost what. Items: Write what you have to spend this week · Put the rest in the calendar first · Stop each task before you have to · Plan a quiet day either side of the big one · Break the one big job into three · Notice the good day for what it is · Keep one short note of what cost what · Say no with the reason left out · Let the plan change without a verdict.

item.title: Facing the Whole Picture of What You Owe
item.description: For the point where you stop guessing and put every debt on one page. It gets the rates in order, finds free advice rather than paid, sets one monthly amount you can actually keep, and separates owing money from what kind of person you are. Items: Write every debt on one page · Put the interest rate beside each one · Call the worst one first and ask for terms · Find the free advice line in your state · Set one amount that leaves the house monthly · Separate the debt from your character · Tell one person the real number · Put the date of the next review in · Stop checking the balance daily.

item.title: When a Family Member Stops Speaking to You
item.description: For a parent, sibling or child who has stopped speaking to you. It keeps the door unlocked without leaving you waiting at it, gets the unsent letter written, settles what to tell people who ask, and expects the anniversaries to hurt. Items: Send one short message, then stop sending · Write the long letter and keep it · Decide what you would apologize for · Ask one relative to carry nothing · Let the anniversaries be hard · Answer the question in public simply · Build the family you do have · Leave the door unlocked, not open.

item.title: Noticing What Went Right Today
item.description: For the end of a day that felt like nothing good happened. It asks for three small things rather than big ones, what it was about them that landed, and one person to actually thank, in two minutes at the same point each day. Items: Write down three small things, not big ones · Say what it was about them that landed · Do it at the same point each day · Include something you did, not only got · Name one person who helped and tell them · Keep it to two minutes · Let a bad day have a short list · Read last week's back on a flat day.

item.title: When Everything Is Too Loud
item.description: For the point in a day when the noise, the light and the people are more than you can take. It cuts one input at a time, gets the ears and the lights down, asks the room for ten minutes, and returns you to one job rather than the list. Items: Cut one input before you fix anything · Put something over your ears for ten minutes · Turn the overhead light down to one lamp · Get the tag, the waistband or the shoes off · Go to the smallest room in the house · Say out loud that you need ten minutes · Put one hand on something cool · Come back to one thing, not the list.

item.title: The Paperwork After a Death
item.description: For the weeks of paperwork that follow a death, when the forms arrive faster than the grief allows. It gets the certificates and the account list in one place, holds the pace to one call a day, and postpones every decision that can wait. Items: Get ten copies of the death certificate · Make one list of every account and policy · Tell the bank and the pension first · Do one call a day, not six · Keep a notebook by the phone · Let someone else make the calls you dread · Say no to any decision that can wait · Expect a form to undo you · Call or text 988 if it gets too heavy.

item.title: Turning the Noise Down on Your Phone
item.description: For when the phone is running your attention rather than the other way around. It turns off the notifications that are not people, moves the worst apps off the first screen, puts the charger outside the bedroom, and keeps one hour a day free of it. Items: Turn off every notification but calls and texts · Take the badge counts off the icons · Move the two worst apps off the first screen · Charge it outside the bedroom tonight · Set one hour a day with no phone in it · Turn the screen to black and white for a week · Unfollow five accounts that leave you flat · Look at the weekly screen time once.

item.title: Giving a Few Hours Away
item.description: For wanting to give some time but never getting past the thought. It starts from a skill you already have, turns a cause into one specific shift, counts the real cost in travel and hours, and allows the whole thing to be for you too. Items: Start from what you already do · Pick a shift, not a cause · Ask how long they need you for · Check what it will actually cost you · Say what you cannot do up front · Expect the first session to be awkward · Let it be for you as well · Stop if it turns into another duty.

item.title: When Good Enough Has to Do
item.description: For the piece of work you keep rewriting past the point of improvement. It gets finished written down as a standard, puts a timer on the last pass, and lets you send the version you have rather than the one you are still imagining. Items: Write down what finished actually means · Set a timer for the last pass · Ask who else will notice the difference · Send the version you have at the deadline · Keep a list of what you would change · Name the fear under the rewriting · Let one thing be visibly ordinary this week · Count sending it as the achievement.

item.title: Getting Back Into Dating
item.description: For getting back out there after a long gap or a bad stretch. It helps you decide what you are looking for, keep the apps to a set time, move to a short meeting early, and read a run of dead ends as the process rather than a verdict. Items: Decide what you are actually looking for · Put one honest photo of your face up · Write a profile line you would say out loud · Give yourself a cap on the apps · Move to a short meeting early · Tell a friend where you are going · Expect most of them to go nowhere · Take a week off when it goes flat · Keep one thing in the week that is not dating.

item.title: The Week You Pack Up a Home
item.description: For the week before a move, when the whole house has to go in boxes. It starts in the room you use least, puts the documents and the first-night things where you can find them, and leaves a chair out until the end. Items: Start with the room you use least · Pack one box of first-night things · Label by room and by urgency · Decide the keep-or-go rule once · Photograph anything you take apart · Put the documents in a bag you carry · Keep one chair and one lamp out till last · Book help for the heavy hour · Say goodbye to the place on purpose.

item.title: Cutting Back on Drinking
item.description: For the weeks you want to drink less without making it a whole identity. It gets the real number written down, names the nights that stay dry, puts a sentence in your pocket for the offer, and treats a slip as information. Items: Write down what you actually drank this week · Pick the nights that stay dry, by name · Decide the number before you go out · Have the first one later than usual · Keep something you like that is not alcohol · Have one sentence ready for the offer · Notice which situation does most of it · Count a slip as data, not a verdict · Tell your doctor if you drink every day.

item.title: Visiting Someone in the Hospital
item.description: For going to see someone in the hospital when you are not sure what helps. It keeps the visit short, puts something useful in your bag, lets them choose the subject, and leaves one concrete offer behind on the way out. Items: Ask before you go rather than surprise them · Plan for twenty minutes, not an afternoon · Bring something small and useful · Sit down at their eye level · Let them steer what gets talked about · Skip the stories about someone else's case · Ask the nurse what helps, not the internet · Offer one concrete thing as you leave · Let yourself feel wrung out afterward.

item.title: Getting Outside After Days Indoors
item.description: For the stretch when you have not been outside in days and the door feels heavier than it is. It sets the bar at the end of the street, puts the first trip in daylight, and asks for five still minutes out there rather than a brisk walk. Items: Set the bar at the end of the street · Go before you are properly dressed for it · Put the first trip in daylight if you can · Pick a route with no errand attached · Or take the long way to something you need · Leave the headphones off for part of it · Sit on a bench instead of turning back · Notice what the air felt like once you are in.

item.title: When a Neighbor Problem Needs Raising
item.description: For the noise, the parking or the fence that has been bothering you for weeks. It gets the specifics down, puts a knock before a note, names the one change that would fix it, and keeps the whole thing off the neighborhood group. Items: Write down the dates and times it happened · Ask whether they could even know it is a problem · Knock before you write a note · Open with the problem, not the person · Say what would fix it in one sentence · Keep it off the neighborhood group · Know your next step before you knock · Decide what you can live with.

item.title: When a Friendship Has Run Its Course
item.description: For a friendship that has quietly thinned out and may be over. It helps you tell a drift from a rift, make one clear attempt before deciding, and let the thing end without turning it into a verdict on either of you. Items: Notice who has been doing the reaching · Ask whether this is a drift or a rift · Make one clear invitation before you decide · Stop keeping score of the silences · Decide whether the ending needs saying out loud · Let it be sad without making it a verdict · Keep what it gave you, not just how it ended · Put the free evening toward someone current.

item.title: Your First Month Retired
item.description: For the first weeks after finishing work, when the days arrive with nothing already in them. It keeps one fixed point in the day, names what the job was giving you besides money, and expects the flat stretch that follows the first excitement. Items: Keep one fixed point in the day · Do not fill the calendar in week one · Name what work gave you besides money · Find one thing with other people in it · Pick one project with no deadline on it · Say the date plainly when asked what you do · Book what work used to crowd out · Expect a flat week somewhere in the middle.

item.title: Getting Back Behind the Wheel
item.description: For getting back to driving after a crash, a near miss, or years out of the driver's seat. It rebuilds the habit in small steps, starting with the parked car and a quiet loop, and adds one new thing at a time rather than all of it at once. Items: Sit in the parked car with the engine off · Drive the same quiet loop three times · Pick the hour with the least traffic · Take someone calm in the passenger seat · Keep the radio off for the first few trips · Know where you could pull over on the route · Add one new thing each time, not three · Say out loud what went fine afterward.

item.title: When You Are Still Carrying a Grudge
item.description: For a resentment you have been carrying for months or years and are tired of. It helps you weigh what it is costing you, tell letting go apart from letting someone back in, and put a boundary where the grudge has been standing in for one. Items: Write down what it has actually cost you · Count how often it still visits your day · Separate letting go from letting back in · Write the letter you are never going to send · Give up on getting the apology first · Decide whether anything still needs saying · Notice what the resentment is protecting · Put the boundary in place instead · Expect it to come back now and then.

item.title: The Day You Fly Somewhere
item.description: For the day you fly when flying is the part you dread. It gets the documents, food and distractions settled early, gives you something to do with your body in the air, and tells the crew you could use an eye kept on you. Items: Put the documents in one pocket the night before · Eat something before you leave for the airport · Pick an aisle seat if you get to choose · Download enough to fill the whole flight · Tell the cabin crew you are a nervous flyer · Breathe out longer than you breathe in on taxi · Learn which noises come when · Keep water and gum with you, not overhead · Plan the first hour after you land.

item.title: Making Room for Something You Enjoy
item.description: For the weeks that are all obligation and nothing you do for its own sake. It helps you name something you used to enjoy, give it a slot and a low bar, and keep it from turning into one more thing to be good at. Items: Name one thing you used to lose hours in · Book twenty minutes for it this week · Get the thing out of its case or box · Let the first go be bad on purpose · Keep it off the internet this week · Do not tie it to getting better at it · Say out loud which evening it is happening · Notice how you feel in the hour afterward.

item.title: When Your Pet Is Ill
item.description: For the weeks an animal you love is sick and the decisions keep coming. It keeps the vet's answers, the costs and the medication times in one place, and treats the worry as real rather than something to apologize for. Items: Write down what you have noticed, with dates · Ask what the next week is likely to look like · Get the cost of each option in writing · Put the medication times on a timer · Set up one room so nothing is a climb · Tell one person who will take it seriously · Keep one piece of your own routine · Write down what a good day looks like for them · Let yourself feel it before anything happens.

item.title: The Hour Before an Interview
item.description: For the hour before an interview, when the preparation is done and the nerves arrive anyway. It settles the practical things early, puts three stories within reach, and gives you something to say if your mind goes blank. Items: Be somewhere nearby twenty minutes early · Read your own application once, not five times · Have three stories ready rather than a script · Write down one question you actually want answered · Drink water and eat something small · Put your phone away before you walk in · Breathe out slowly for a count of six · Decide now what you will say if you blank · Plan the first thing you do when it ends.

item.title: Telling Your Child Something Hard
item.description: For the news you have to give a child — a separation, a death, a move, a diagnosis in the family — and the hour before you say it. It helps you decide what to tell them, keep it in their language, and leave room for whatever comes back. Items: Decide the one sentence they need first · Pick a time that is not bedtime or a school morning · Say it in words they already use · Tell them plainly that it is not their fault · Say what will stay the same for them · Let the silence sit without filling it · Answer the question asked, not the whole thing · Tell their teacher or another adult tomorrow.

item.title: The Night Before a Procedure
item.description: For the evening before an operation or a procedure, when the instructions are long and the mind is loud. It helps you get the practical things done early, set up the day after, and give the fear somewhere to go before lights out. Items: Read the instructions again and write the times · Pack the bag tonight, not in the morning · Confirm who is taking you and collecting you · Put food and easy meals in for afterward · Write your questions on your phone now · Tell one person what time it starts · Say the frightening thought out loud once · Put something undemanding on until you sleep.

item.title: When Washing Feels Like Too Much
item.description: For the stretch where showering, teeth and clean clothes have all slid, and the longer it goes the harder it gets. It helps you pick the smallest version of each, lower the bar on purpose, and get one thing done without a verdict attached. Items: Pick one thing only, not the whole list · Use the wipes, dry shampoo or mouthwash · Sit down in the shower if standing is too much · Put clean clothes where you will see them · Set a two-minute limit and stop at it · Put something loud on while you do it · Skip the catch-up on everything you missed · Tell someone if this has lasted weeks.

item.title: Facing the Paperwork You Keep Avoiding
item.description: For the form, claim or renewal that has been on the kitchen table for a month and grows heavier every time you walk past. It helps you find out what it actually needs, do one piece of it today, and stop the deadline from arriving first. Items: Read it once and write the deadline down · List what you need to gather, not what to do · Find the hardest document first · Fill in only the boxes you can answer now · Call the number on it with your question · Book twenty minutes for it in the calendar · Do it at a table, not on your phone · Put it in the mail or hit send the same day.

item.title: Getting Back in Touch After Too Long
item.description: For the friend you have been meaning to message for a year and now feel awkward about. It helps you send something rather than nothing, say the quiet part about the gap, and leave the ball in a place where it can actually come back. Items: Send it today rather than drafting it perfectly · Name the silence in one line, then move on · Skip the apology beyond a sentence · Mention one specific thing you remember · Offer a concrete time, not a vague catch-up · Accept a short reply as a good outcome · Let one unanswered message be the end of it · Put a reminder in for three months.

item.title: When a Project Stalls Halfway
item.description: For the thing you were excited about two months ago and have not touched in three weeks. It helps you work out whether it stalled from boredom, overwhelm or a wrong turn, and pick the one small step that gets it moving again. Items: Write where it actually stopped, not why · Ask whether it is boring, too big, or wrong · Cut the next step down to twenty minutes · Do the ugly version of the next piece · Decide out loud whether you still want it · Put one working session in the calendar · Tell someone the next step and the date · Shrink the finish line if it has drifted.

item.title: When a Bill You Cannot Pay Arrives
item.description: For the letter or email that asks for money you do not have right now. It helps you find out what is actually owed and by when, make the call before the deadline passes, and keep the fear from turning into weeks of unopened mail. Items: Open it and write down the amount and the date · Check whether it is a final notice or a first one · Call them before the date, not after · Ask directly for a payment plan or an extension · List what else is due this month, in order · Look up free debt advice in your state · Tell one person the actual number · Put the next unopened letter on today's list.

item.title: Five Minutes in the Middle of a Bad Day
item.description: For a day that has gone wrong by eleven in the morning and still has hours left in it. It helps you take a deliberate break instead of pushing through on fumes, and decide what the rest of the day actually has to contain. Items: Stop mid-task rather than at a finish line · Leave the room you have been sitting in · Put the phone in a drawer for the five minutes · Drink a full glass of water slowly · Look at something more than ten feet away · Say what has actually gone wrong in one sentence · Cross one thing off the afternoon on purpose · Go back in on the easiest thing left.

item.title: When Someone Else's Good News Stings
item.description: For the moment a friend's promotion, engagement or baby announcement lands with a thud instead of joy. It helps you let the feeling pass without acting on it, answer them like someone who cares, and look at what the sting is pointing at. Items: Say the ugly reaction to yourself once · Send the congratulations anyway, briefly · Wait a day before you post anything · Close the app for the rest of the evening · Name what you actually want underneath it · Write one step toward that thing this month · List two things going well for you now · Tell one honest person how it landed.

item.title: When the Dark Comes Earlier
item.description: For the weeks when it is dark before you finish work and the evenings stretch out. It helps you get light early, keep something in the calendar each week, and notice the slide before it has taken the whole season. Items: Get outside within an hour of waking · Eat lunch by a window or outdoors · Put one thing in the calendar for each week · Turn on lamps before it gets dark, not after · Keep the walk you had in summer, shorter · Hold your wake-up time steady on weekends · Write down how you felt in January last year · Tell your doctor if this happens every year.

item.title: A Day When Your Body Hurts
item.description: For the days pain or illness sets the terms and the plans have to shrink. It helps you cut the day down to what matters, ask for the help you would rather not ask for, and get through it without adding guilt to the pile. Items: Pick the one thing that has to happen today · Cancel or move one thing before noon · Ask one person for one specific thing · Set your medication and water within reach · Put something on that needs nothing from you · Change position or get outside for five minutes · Write down what today was like for your next visit · Drop the ledger of what you did not do.

item.title: When You Owe Someone an Apology
item.description: For when you know you were in the wrong and the longer you leave it the worse it gets. It helps you work out what to say, say it without a defense attached, and then let the other person decide what happens next. Items: Write down the specific thing you did · Cut every sentence starting with because · Say what it cost them, not what you meant · Name one thing you will do differently · Do it today, in the way they prefer · Ask nothing of them in the same breath · Sit with the silence afterward · Stop retelling it to yourself tonight.

item.title: Your First Week in a New Job
item.description: For the week you start somewhere new, when everybody else knows how things work and you do not. It helps you learn names, ask the questions that feel too basic to ask later, and judge yourself on the right things for a while. Items: Write down names and roles the day you hear them · Ask the basic questions now, not in a month · Find out what your manager counts as a good first month · Book a short chat with two people on your team · Keep a list of what confused you today · Leave on time at least three days this week · Judge yourself on learning, not output · Tell someone at home how it is going.

item.title: After a Rejection You Did Not Expect
item.description: For the hours after a no you were not braced for, from a job, an application or a person. It helps you get through the first evening, keep the no from spreading into a verdict on you, and work out what, if anything, to do next. Items: Say the sentence plainly to yourself once · Hold off replying for a day · Tell one person the same evening · Write what this no is actually about · Name one thing you did well regardless · Eat and sleep as normally as you can manage · Ask for feedback once, then let it be · Pick the next small step for later in the week.

item.title: Getting Through a Family Visit
item.description: For the holiday weekend or the trip home where the old patterns are waiting. It helps you decide beforehand what you will and will not get into, build in time away from the room, and leave without a week of regret. Items: Decide the two topics you will not discuss · Book your own transport there and back · Pick an end time before you arrive · Have one sentence ready to change the subject · Take a walk or an errand halfway through · Text one person outside the family during the day · Pick one person you are glad to see · Plan something easy for the evening you get back.

item.title: The Week You Are Waiting on News
item.description: For the stretch between a test, an application or a decision and the answer, when nothing you do changes the outcome. It helps you put the waiting somewhere, keep the days usable, and stop rehearsing every version of the result. Items: Find out when the answer actually comes · Set one time a day to check for it · Write the worst outcome and your first three steps · Stop researching once you have what you need · Put something in the calendar for each day · Tell one person you are waiting · Move your body once a day, even briefly · Notice when you are rehearsing and name it.
